answer_text:
lantern-tundra-526

The documents describe how to install and run Strata, a local model server for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on NVIDIA or AMD GPUs, exposing OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints on `http://127.0.0.1:8080`. The AI_SETUP guide stresses safety: never expose the server without an API key; `--host 0.0.0.0` must be paired with `--api-key`. It outlines hardware checks: NVIDIA RTX 20/30/40/50 or AMD RX 7900/7800/7700/9060/9070/R9700/RX 6800-6900, ≥12 GB VRAM, 32 GB RAM, ~80 GB disk, AVX2 CPU. Model selection depends on RAM: `--family coder --model IQ1_M` for 32 GB, `qwen IQ2_XS` for 48–64 GB, `IQ3_S` for 96 GB+, or `unsloth UD-IQ4_XS`. Setup flags include `--yes`, `--family`, `--model`, `--context`, `--vision`, `--gpu`, `--backend`, `--data-dir`, `--port`, and `--no-start`; `--no-start` is recommended for agents. The server is verified with `/health`, `/v1/models`, and chat completions. Troubleshooting covers old drivers, port conflicts, RAM/VRAM pressure, page-file settings, and AMD detection.

The AMD_HIP document details HIP backend support for gfx1100/1101/1200/1201/1030. On Linux, setup uses the kernel amdgpu driver, optionally system ROCm 7 or installs AMD TheRock ROCm wheels into `.venv` (~10 GB), then compiles the engine for the card architecture (10–20 minutes). It can use hipBLASLt tuning tables when versions match, and supports multi-GPU layer splitting. On Windows, a ready-made engine zip bundles ROCm; no compiler/admin is needed, but one card per model and no vision on Windows. Known issues include Windows HIP runtime DLL conflicts, VRAM budget quirks, and desktop GPU memory pressure; `--vram-reserve-mib` mitigates the latter. Both guides emphasize local-only operation, resumable downloads, and verification before app integration.
